We investigated connectable branes based on generalized $\lambda$-deformations, which are connected to groupmanifolds, incorporating a key feature of Deiflt shifts, utilizing the sl2 WZW model as a foundational example. The deformation's key parameters were found to have straightforward interpretations in string theory's context. Our research revealed that the string theory's worldsheet conformal dimension remains unchanged under deformation for specific states, a fact also observed in other deformations. We found that for states with zero momentum, a conformally relevant direction emerges only when a certain condition, involving angles and deformation parameters, is met. Our research also showed that for specific deformations based on specific cosets, a conformally relevant direction emerges at a certain angle, provided the deformation parameters fall within a certain range. We found that for specific deformations based on specific cosets, a conformally irrelevant direction emerges at a condition, involving angles and deformation parameters, and also that the vacuum becomes marginal at a condition, involving deformation parameters. We found that for specific deformations based on specific cosets, a conformally irrelevant direction emerges at a condition, involving deformation parameters, involving specific deformation parameters, involving specific deformation parameters.

One of the primary hurdles in using hexahedral meshes for finite element analysis and other applications lies in their difficult-to-handle nature compared to triangular meshes. Although hexahedral meshes offer a significant reduction in the number of degrees of freedom, their poor discretization often leads to diminished performance. To achieve good performance, it is crucial to handle the interfaces between tetrahedra and hexahedra effectively. A new Tet/Hex interface formulation has been developed to address this issue by splitting hexahedra into two internal and one external tetrahedra in a way that preserves symmetry and prevents numerical artifacts. This formulation includes novel interface matrices specifically designed for hexahedral elements by analyzing their symmetry properties under different numerical quadrature rules. When applied to standard higher-order Lagrange elements, it outperforms the traditional approach of simply gluing tetrahedra and hexahedra together and even the cutting method proposed by Henshaw and Thompson in 1988. Moreover, its performance surpasses that of purely hexahedral meshes composed of one hexahedron per reference element and approaches that of purely tetrahedral meshes.

The task of relation extraction (RE) involves utilizing a pre annotated text to determine the existing relationships between specified entities.  This paper introduces a novel approach to RE by integrating it with knowledge graph link prediction (KGLP), an unannotated task that makes predictions about the links between entities based on existing knowledge graph data.  By combining RE and KGLP, we can enhance the performance of RE by leveraging the benefits of unannotated data and knowledge graph information.  To achieve this, we first fine-tune a knowledge graph embedding model using the available unannotated knowledge, and subsequently employ it to generate predictions for the links between entities.  Finally, we integrate the link predictions generated by the model with the pre annotated text to develop a knowledge-grounded RE model that outperforms the current state-of-the-art models in RE by utilizing a comprehensive array of knowledge graph embedding models.

The rise of online streaming services has made audio converter delay a crucial factor in achieving seamless user experience for a wide variety of audio file conversions. This paper proposes an analytical model for predicting converter delay as a function of file size and per-sample processing time. Initially, we propose an method of using the Curve Fitting Toolkit in Matlab to create delay models from sample processing times and corresponding processing times. Next, we propose a method of deriving 'standard' delay models for 16-bit, 44 kHz, two-channel PCM audio. Furthermore, we evaluate the accuracy of these models through comparative analysis.

We explore the fundamental properties of the value function in the context of the generalized Markov decision process (gMDP). Our findings indicate that under a contraction mapping, the value function exhibits semi-continuity in the lower and semi-continuity in the upper, provided the reward function and the transition kernel satisfy certain conditions. These conditions can be viewed as the coarse-grained versions of the standard assumptions found in the theory of Markov decision processes in the weak topology. To validate the applicability of our results, we examine the value function in various gMDP settings involving the classification and reinforcement learning. Our research also includes a discussion on the limitations imposed by the topology of the state space and how our findings can be extended to the more general MDPs beyond the gMDP framework.

Research has demonstrated that the pattern of neuronal connections within the temporal lobe is closely linked to how humans recognize and categorize objects. A recent study by Bengio et al. (2009) found that deeper layers of the temporal cortex support increasingly complex notions of reality. In this paper, we delve into these findings by developing a series of automated models inspired by human knowledge of various domains. These models start with basic features and gradually incorporate abstract concepts at higher levels. We then test these models against a large dataset of images in an effort to replicate human understanding. Our results confirm the existence of the animacy structure, as well as provide insights into its underlying mechanisms. Notably, we discovered that domain-specific visual cues play a crucial role in shaping these models' performance. Moreover, our research reveals that the progress from lower to higher-level concepts follows a distinct curve, as opposed to linear growth. These findings contribute to our understanding of how humans and artificial systems navigate the complexities of visual recognition and categorization.

In electromagnetic and acoustic engineering simulations, the flow tangential boundary condition plays a significant role, particularly in modeling fluid flows, electric currents, and acoustic waves. The traditional approach utilizes finite difference methods on structured grids with local super-time-stepping techniques. However, numerical instabilities can arise when the computational time step exceeds a certain threshold due to the numerical Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (FCFL) limitation. To address this issue, our proposed method involves developing a global super-time-stepping scheme coupled with an innovative high-order arrangement-preserving (AP) filter designed to mitigate oscillations near sharp gradients. By formulating an optimization problem involving second-derivative-based curvature penalties and its Hessian matrix, the proposed AP filter enables efficient and flexible implementation in multidimensional parallel simulations.

In this study, researchers used data from the Astro-H and Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer to detect quasi-periodic oscillations in X-ray emissions from the microquasar MAX J1535-571 during a 2018 outburst. They identified two distinct states of quasi-periodical fluctuations, referred to as A and B, within a specific time frame. State A occurred during a period of intense activity, while state B emerged after a period of low activity. By comparing the characteristics of these two states, researchers found evidence that state B exhibited features of a hard state that was not present in state A. Furthermore, they discovered that the period of quasi-periodic oscillations in state B was shorter than in state A, while after the emergence of state B, the distance of the corona from the accretion disk was found to be significantly smaller. These findings suggest that the development of state B was accompanied by a significant change in the structure of the accretion disk and the establishment of a thinner disk that was eventually disrupted.

A key challenge in building social robots as partners for humans lies in their consistent performance of desired behaviors over extended periods. The unpredictability of human behavior, many-to-many behavior mappings, and the constantly evolving nature of these interactions make it difficult to forecast future actions accurately. Moreover, when a social robot's established behavior ceases to be effective, it must promptly adapt to the new situation. In this study, we introduce a novel method called Social Transfer Empowerment (STE) to empower robots with reliable behaviors, and enable them to transfer and transfer these behaviors effectively to new tasks. Our approach leverages social rewards and rewards the continuity of social behaviors, thereby helping the robot reliably learn its assigned role. To facilitate adaptability, we employ a meta-controller that guides the robot to transfer behaviors to new contexts, which we validate using a NAO humanoid robot in a Marbles & Pursuit game. Our findings show that our proposed method successfully enables the robot to consistently fulfill its role, transfer its behavior to a new game, and adapt its behavior to accommodate partner changes.

Current substance identification methods rely on specific, pre-defined contexts and require extensive, labeled data. A new machine learning model, inspired by contrastive learning, enables identification of any substance given an image of its plasma spectrum in a specific environment. A high-level 2D plasma simulation generates synthetic spectra and labels, allowing the development of a universal recognizer capable of distinguishing substances from solar spectra and impurities. By training a simple neural network on a vast set of synthetic examples, the model achieves exceptional accuracy, recognizing substances as small as diatomic molecules. Contrastive loss maximizes spectral uniqueness and spectral variability across the dataset. A comparison of reconstruction and likelihood-based approaches reveals the superiority of contrastive learning for a classification task. To facilitate its application, a Python package enables the generation of synthetic spectra and training data.

Lie 2-algebras constitute a specific type of 2-algebra, which can be viewed as a categorification of Lie algebras, with their definition equivalent to Lie algebras that are also categorified. This concept holds significance across multiple perspectives within higher category theory. In this survey, we provide an in-depth, self-contained derivation of Lie 2-algebras through various approaches and discuss their key characteristics and applications.

We introduce a novel, detector-free method called LoFTR, designed to locally align keypoints between images by using a self-attention Transformer network to produce a joint feature map, point descriptors, and point displacements in a unified manner. By training LoFTR with a loss function that minimizes geometric consistency, we achieve a robust model capable of handling diverse and challenging real-world scenes. Unlike traditional methods, our approach does not rely on keypoint detection, thereby avoiding the introduction of biases associated with different keypoint detectors. We evaluate the effectiveness of LoFTR on various tasks, including video pose estimation, 3D reconstruction, and SLAM, and demonstrate its superiority to state-of-the-art detectors and correlation networks through comprehensive experiments, particularly in semi-structured scenes.

This paper aims to explore and address potential biases in the measurement of solar vector magnetic fields through specific methods. A notable technique, Least Absolute Deviations, has been found to introduce a notable bias by underestimating magnetic field measurements, particularly during periods of rapid change. This underestimation becomes more pronounced as the period of data change increases. To counter this issue, we propose utilizing Gaussian measurements to determine magnetic fields due to their lack of bias. Additionally, we investigate alternative techniques, such as Kalman filtering, that demonstrate minimal bias. A calibrated vector solar magnetic field data product developed through a Kalman filtering method shows a considerable improvement in accuracy compared to the product generated using Least Absolute Deviations, exhibiting differences of approximately 15% during periods of rapid data change.

A novel approach to independent demand side control is developed to mitigate real-time electricity charges without compromising consumer comfort. The proposed strategy employs a game-theoretic framework wherein each consumer utilizes a planning method to distribute their real-time energy load charging across available time slots. The objective of this experiment lies in validating the feasibility of implementing a non-intrusive, decentralized control strategy.

A recent analysis focused on the properties of charged black holes in the Rastai gravity framework, specifically the impact of electromagnetic properties on these systems. We conducted a comparative examination of the thermodynamic characteristics of the previously studied case against those of their neutral counterparts. This investigation revealed the presence of additional constraints in both temperature and heat capacity for these black holes. By investigating the relationship between the electromagnetic and gravitational forces, we discovered the existence of a critical point where these forces balance each other and identified this point's behavior as a function of the observer's altitude. A detailed comparison of this equilibrium point with that of their uncharged counterparts also showed that both are related in a universal manner for all black holes in the astrophysical universe. This research has significant implications for understanding the relationship between the properties of compact objects and their corresponding gravitational and electromagnetic interactions in the cosmological context. We further explored the possibility that the existence of the cosmological constant in the Rastai gravity theory could be a function of the matter properties, specifically for both perfect fluids and electromagnetic fields. We found that a relationship between the electromagnetic and gravitational properties exists, and this relationship is characterized by the existence of a finite and positive value of the matter parameter that balances the electromagnetic and gravitational properties in the cosmological context.

We derive precise mathematical expressions for both the empirical spectral distribution and the modified empirical spectral distribution of finite real symmetric matrices representing stochastic diffusion processes derived from Markov chains. We then analyze the speed of convergence for the empirical spectral distribution towards the equilibrium spectral distribution in the context of the finite von Neumann ergodic theorem. Additionally, we establish an explicit formula for the drift factor $1-\lambda_2(P)$, where $\lambda_2(P)$ is the second largest eigenvalue of $P$. We apply our findings to specific examples, including random regular graphs, Laplacian Hessian matrices, and Erdos-Renyi graph models.

The majority of stars in the Milky Way are metal-poor stars, which include globular cluster stars, the halo, and the outer disk populations, such as the ancient stellar populations. Determining the metallicity of stars is crucial for understanding their formation and the galaxy as a whole. A newly developed method has been created to estimate the metallicity of metal-poor stars using the full spectrum data available from the Gaia mission, covering the range of wavelengths from 485.9 to 677.0 nanometers. This method has been applied and tested with a sample of 1,247 stars and found to be accurate, with a mean metallicity difference of 0.0005 ± 0.0002 dex from spectroscopic measurements and 0.06 dex in the stars with the lowest metallicity levels. This method has the potential to estimate the metallicity of up to 100,000 stars, providing valuable insights into the galaxy's ancient stellar populations.

Every year, wildfires肆虐 across the globe, causing widespread destruction of lives and property and emitting large amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. A novel machine learning approach is introduced to evaluate the intensity of wildfires worldwide, based on the number of active fires within a specific geographical area and time frame. It builds upon existing fire monitoring systems utilizing satellite data and weather observations. It performs exceptionally well and achieves high accuracy compared to existing methodologies, thereby providing valuable insights into wildfire management and resource allocation. Furthermore, this model aids in understanding regional patterns of fire behavior and may serve as a tool for resource managers to make more informed decisions.

Language complexity research has primarily relied on corpus metrics, but the meaning behind these measures remains unclear, and there's no standardized approach for creating or validating them. This study examines and compares various lexicon-based complexity indicators through two different methods. Firstly, it evaluates the relationships and correlations of these measures against each other and against established complexity indicators (MorphoLex and WordNet) to determine how they interconnect. The results indicate strong correlations, suggesting the metrics may be measuring the same aspect of language, but it's uncertain what exactly they're measuring. The second part of the study employs novel psycholinguistic data to assess and validate the metrics' ability to accurately represent their target of measurement. The analysis reveals that the chosen metrics don't accurately account for the difficulty of language processing, implying they may not be effectively measuring processing complexity. The study concludes by offering recommendations for future research to develop and validate new complexity metrics, and it investigates the potential causes of these metrics' lack of effectiveness.

Galaxy cluster core regions and those forming in the outskirts of their host galaxies exhibit distinct characteristics, characterized by a compact distribution of bright galaxies surrounded by diffuse, diffuse galaxy light. These areas, termed core regions and gravitational magnifiers respectively, are believed to be the result of prolonged interactions between these objects and their environment. Core regions, in particular, are believed to host highly concentrated and distorted objects, displaying strong gravitational magnification effects. 

Recent research suggests a strong link between gravitational magnifiers and the presence of dark matter self-interactions, where these interactions cause dark matter to settle in the core regions of their host galaxies. As a result, light from the surrounding interstellar medium shifts towards these core regions in response to self-interactions.

Our study aims to further investigate the relationship between gravitational magnifiers and self-interacting dark matter. We analyze the distribution of gravitational magnifiers across 18 galaxy clusters and their host galaxies, where 13 of these objects are located within their host cores and 5 in the surrounding low-density regions. Our research reveals that gravitational magnifiers exhibit a preference for the core regions of galaxy clusters, where self-interacting dark matter is predicted to accumulate. Furthermore, our data indicates a higher likelihood of core concentration in clusters hosting gravitationally distorted objects, where these interactions cause dark matter to accumulate in the core regions.

Our research also shows that self-interacting dark matter causes galaxy clusters to exhibit compact, dense structures. We find that these interactions cause dark matter

Model compression techniques have been developed to reduce the complexity and improve the efficiency of neural networks, but most methods focus on the network's output. A new model compression method from the perspective of partial observations has been proposed, using observations as masks for pruning a neural network. A theoretical framework for understanding the relationship between masked submodels and observation masks has been developed and used to guide model compression. The proposed method, known as MEDEA, prunes a neural network by optimizing an empirical risk minimization objective. The results of experiments on image classification and autoencoder tasks show that the method successfully reduces the size of neural networks while maintaining accuracy, and is effective even with random masks.

M-ark learning techniques have become a standard method for nonlinear independent component analysis in fields such as signal processing and statistics. M-ark techniques employ iterative algorithms, known as rapid mixing, which converge to local optima. Certain statistics, influenced by scores and functions of scores, have been found effective in identifying and separating independent components. We generate simulated data sets to investigate the impact of score functions on nonlinear separation performance. Moreover, the influence of data dimensionality and sample size on separation performance is also examined. We demonstrate that incorporating score functions significantly enhances the nonlinear separation performance and that optimized score functions can increase the convergence rate of certain algorithms.

Real-time traffic incident monitoring is essential for minimizing accidents and congestion. Social media platforms like Foursquare and Twitter provide incident information, but existing systems struggle to process this information effectively in a fast-paced environment. Our work introduces a novel approach to identify traffic incidents geotagged on social media platforms by analyzing the spatial density of relevant updates over short time intervals. By employing clustering techniques and analyzing critical boundaries, our method pinpointed 281 traffic incidents in Los Angeles, accounting for 93% of observed incidents during peak hours. Our proposed density-based spatio-temporal incident identification technique enables real-time incident detection and accurate traffic simulation, ultimately facilitating traffic management and congestion avoidance.

This research focuses on the following fractional-type elliptic equation: $$ -\Delta u = \mu \quad \text{in } \Omega $$ where the domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^N$ ($N \geq 2$) contains points on a $(N-1)$-dimensional smooth surface $\Sigma$. The measure $\mu$ is supported on $\Sigma$. We examine the implications of this equation given specific surface $\Sigma$ and measure $\mu$. We particularly analyze how this equation relates to the classical Poisson equation when the fractional parameter $s$ approaches 1 from below.

We've successfully leveraged the generative capabilities of a long-short term memory network to create a long-list of promising cobalt-rich compounds within the yttrium-cobalt-boron system. By utilizing an energetic model specifically designed for this system, we've filtered out unstable candidates, leaving us with 19 novel cobalt-abundant Y-Co-B compounds that require experimental verification. Given cobalt's significant role in various technological advancements, our proposed approach offers a versatile solution for discovering new functional materials across multiple fields such as magnetism, magneto-caloric effects, and magnetic storage, among others.

Real-world online scenarios often involve risk-sensitive problems, where decision-makers consider both potential rewards and risks in addition to optimal utility maximization. For instance, in real-world bidding scenarios, advertisers have a budget to work within and balance their profit and loss. Current research on risk-sensitive problems often focuses on continuous risk metrics like Negative Exponential Risk. However, numerous applications prefer to use the Most Unlucky Risk, a discrete risk metric. Solving risk-sensitive problems with a limited budget within the theory framework is extremely difficult, even more so with continuous risk metrics. We have developed a series of innovative risk-sensitive bidding algorithms that can effectively maximize ad revenue within a limited budget, using either the Negative Exponential Risk or the Most Unlucky Risk. Notably, our algorithms can handle diverse risk preferences and theoretical scenarios, and through a combination of theoretical analysis and real-world testing, demonstrate superior performance over existing solutions.

Regions with negative values in the Wigner function are believed to be essential for creating quantum technologies, yet recent theories suggest they aren't necessary. Our study aims to contradict this prevailing notion by demonstrating the Wigner negativity requirement through its application in universal quantum cloning. A quantum channel lacking specific noise characteristics stemming from the Wigner function's negative regions can't replicate any highly entangled state. Our findings also highlight the Wigner function's capacity to measure the degree of entanglement in two-part systems and reveal the minimum amount of negativity needed in these states for successful cloning.

Quantum key distribution systems that rely on privacy amplification techniques to enhance security often face challenges due to imperfect random number generators, resulting in unevenly distributed expansion bit sources. In our study, we develop a theory for evaluating the information interference between imperfectly distributed erasure channels, which corrupts quantum non-local correlations. This theory is specifically applied to the distribution of privacy amplification bits and their impact on secure key generation rates in the binary quantum discord model, which takes into account the randomness characteristics of privacy amplification sources. Furthermore, we incorporate a practical model for privacy amplification sources, represented by the two-outcome mixed Gaussian distribution, to provide a more comprehensive understanding. In a typical scenario, our theory shows that one-way communication suffices for extracting pre-shared keys. In contrast, its application to the SK key distribution protocol, which employs the six-state protocol, also yields a secure key generation rate that closely matches upper bound rates obtained through brute-force attacks.

This research paper investigates the conditions under which a one-parameter family of timelike curves in three-dimensional R^3_1 satisfies both distance and geodesic constraints, also examining the constant curvature and average curvatures of such curves.

Recent research breakthroughs involving stochastic combinations and sampling distributions of self-intersecting random walks conducted by Barbour, Last, and Nikolayevsky have significantly expanded our analytical tools. Building on these findings, our work investigates novel outcomes related to the collective distributions of Feller diffusions, focusing specifically on the Brownian motion under the influence of a Poisson point process, Feller diffusion driven by a Poisson random measure, as well as innovations stemming from stable Feller diffusions. These investigations will provide the foundational framework for future studies into the behavioral analysis of coalescent trees, leveraging the concept of genealogical structure.

We introduce a new diagrammatic method to evaluate scattering amplitudes of multi-photon states in quantum dot-waveguide systems. This method employs a set of basic rules based on the fundamental interactions between qubits and photons. When diagrammatic amplitudes are calculated, they can be directly related to one another, revealing the underlying relationships between different scattering processes. Our findings demonstrate that the relative phases of diagrammatic amplitudes adhere to universal rules, independent of the specific system configuration. We apply this method to study single and multiple qubit scattering scenarios and compare the results with previous studies. Furthermore, we use the method to analyze the scattering behavior of qubit arrays in both linear and two-dimensional geometries. Our work reveals that the diagrammatic method can effectively capture the fundamental principles of quantum coherence and connectivity in qubit arrays. In addition, we discover that non-local quantum interactions can emerge due to a combination of multiple qubit couplings, opening up new possibilities for information processing in multi-qubit systems.

In the standard cosmological model, two key factors contribute to the large-scale structure of the universe: the cold dark matter and dark energy. Researchers have recently explored the concept of dark matter with particle properties, particularly how its behavior affects cosmological processes. One of the primary properties of dark matter under consideration is how it interacts with spins, a phenomenon referred to as spin-dependent dark matter. To investigate this, scientists examined the relationship between spin-dependent parameters and dark energy, predicting that such a connection would influence the large-scale structure of the universe. To test this hypothesis, the researchers developed a mathematical model that incorporates the spin-dependent parameters, and then simulated the evolution of large-scale structure using modified Newtonian simulations. By comparing their results to observational data, the researchers found that modified dark matter simulations can be consistent with observations when specific conditions are met, particularly concerning the amplitude of halo power and gravitational lensing. Furthermore, researchers discovered that spin-dependent parameters can be constrained by observing the large-scale structure of the universe and such constraints may be further improved through future observations.

This note aims to eulacerate the renowned mathematician Leonhard Euler, and also to promote his contributions and promote his contributions in a field that's underexplored: his contributions to the formula for the sum of the first n pth powers, which was first formalized by Johann Faulhaber.

For a given modulation index, a two-tone continuous phase modulation (CPM) scheme offers superior error correction capabilities compared to a single-tone CPM with differential detection, equivalent to the well-established $4D$ differential phase shift keying (DPSK). Nonetheless, when the DPSK is compared to a two-tone, four-symbol differential demapping technique, it falls short in performance. Interestingly, when used in conjunction with advanced coding methods, DPSK offers relatively low interleaving requirements. This study proposes an alternative two-tone demapping strategy with expanded memory length. Notably, when integrated with sophisticated coding methods, it necessitates significantly reduced interleaving requirements than DPSK, yielding notable gains in DPSK's original demapping schemes. The study presents results showing that this enhanced delay-based demapper achieves substantial diversity order enhancement over its DPSK counterpart. Specifically, it shows a reduction in interleaving requirements by nearly half for a two-tone modulation and a factor of four for a four-tone modulation. This paper provides both theoretical and simulated evidence of its findings.

A novel reward learning technique called VECoRaR is presented, which addresses reward shaping concerns in policy learning. This approach leverages human perception expertise by using a dataset of expert-demonstrated behaviors to create reward functions through clustering and visual inspection. This human-in-the-loop process is aimed at enhancing model learning efficiency and accuracy, ultimately enabling robots to perform complex tasks autonomously. The VECoRaR method is demonstrated on a robotic arm to automatically create cluster reward functions applicable to both linear and nonlinear systems, significantly reducing sample requirements for optimal performance.

This study examines configuration space nucleon amplitudes within noncommutative space-time, focusing particularly on how the Chernoff function influences spatial and momentum space properties. We investigate the impact of noncommutativity on various spin states and discuss how these effects might be identified through deep inelastic scattering experiments, both two and three point, with an eventual consideration of how noncommutativity influences the structure functions we will later define.

We examine a variations of the Toric code on a heptagonal-hexagonal-hexagonal-hexagonal-hexagonal-hexagonal honeycomb lattice where heptagons are centrally embedded within hexagon clusters. Due to heptagonal incorporation, loops encompassing central heptagons fail to commute with star operators, resulting in disrupted logical qubit protection against local errors. Introducing dimer boundary conditions mitigates this issue, yet the topological structure remains vulnerable to states involving dimer boundary cycles under thermal fluctuations. Introducing frustration into dimer boundary conditions disrupts these thermal states, yielding models featuring topological edge modes along non-trivial cycles along with residual stability against local errors.

We consider large, randomly constructed N-by-N band matrices with sparse long-range correlations, where certain entries are perturbed according to a randomly parameterized function f. As the matrix size N becomes infinitely large, this model undergoes a phase transition when the filling parameter d and the functional deformation f interact. Our main result demonstrates that this transition can be accurately modeled using a simplified two-dimensional random potential known as the "Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble" model. This simplified model captures the critical behavior of the original band matrix problem at the transition point, which is further illustrated by detailed examples. This simplified model can be used to further analyze the behavior of the original band matrix problem as it approaches the transition point.

The success of pre-trained language models in conversation comprehension tasks has led to the assumption that their semantic representations have significant value. However, our investigation reveals that these models may rely heavily on syntactic patterns, particularly in complex conversation comprehension tasks. To address this limitation, we propose a pre-training method that incorporates semantic representations and discourse connectives to improve the models' understanding of contextual meanings. Our approach uses a masked semantic prediction task and the structural relationships between discourse units rather than word-level connections. As a result, our proposed model significantly outperforms strong baseline models in complex conversation comprehension tasks.

Many people, beyond just data scientists, rely on automated decision-making, driven by a desire for understanding and trust in these algorithms. To meet this need for interpretation, we propose a framework called Human Learning Orientation (HLO) that considers the learning process of humans when it comes to understanding algorithms. This framework identifies key elements that affect how easily people can learn and comprehend these algorithms. To measure these characteristics, we introduce the concept of Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS), which we use to evaluate a state-of-the-art algorithmic tool called t-SNE through human feedback.

The Isolation Forest is a well-established algorithm for detecting anomalies, but its high computation and memory demands make it impractical for mobile devices and edge-based artificial intelligence systems. Our research presents TiWS-iForest, a more streamlined and lightweight anomaly detection method based on the Isolation Forest, that is better suited to resource-limited systems. By integrating feature selection, reducing isolation tree depth, and optimizing the use of weights and weak learners, TiWS-iForest significantly lowers memory usage and computational time while maintaining strong anomaly detection capabilities. Our experiments show that TiWS-iForest outperforms existing lightweight systems in terms of performance and efficiency, achieving substantial reductions in memory usage of up to 98.7% and computational time of up to 95.7%. Additionally, we have made TiWS-iForest available in a C-based library and source code, enabling seamless deployment on edge devices and mobile platforms.

This study introduces a Bayesian time-reparameterized Poisson process model for point process observations, where the first focal parameter helps determine the rate of event occurrence and the second shapes the time between events, both of which are evaluated using simulated and real-world datasets.

The concepts of "optimal" or "best" are frequently employed to describe things that aren't necessarily the most extreme options. In theoretical physics, researchers often seek solutions that have "local optimality" - a standard that's less definitive than "best" but still more than a casual description, typically associated with "area of stability." In quantum mechanics, the average cross section is a significant physical quantity and understanding its stationary values can be crucial for identifying significant poles in the S-matrix, which have been particularly important in theoretical physics since the 1960s. In this paper, the definition of stationary values of the cross section is revisited using scattering theory, emphasizing the importance of resonance phenomena and underscoring their association with stationary values of cross section. The significance of resonances in understanding the forces that govern particle interactions has been highlighted through historical examples, including the concept of "compound nuclei" and "quasistates."

The purpose of this paper is to present significant advancements in the COMET-ATOMIC network, specifically COMET-ATOMIC 2.0 and its specialized sub-network, COMET-ATOMIC 2.0 Sub-. These advancements encompass the evolution of COMET-KGE 2.0 into COMET-KGE-Net-.0 Sub-, the enhancement of ATOMIC into ATOMIC-Q, the improvement of COMET-ATOMIC 2.0 to COMET-ATOMIC 2.0 Sub-, and COMET-KGE-Net-.0 Q into COMET-KGE-Net-.0 Q, as well as the creation of COMET-ATOMIC 2.0 Rel-. These enhancements specifically integrate the qualities of relationship extraction and knowledge enhancement. Furthermore, this paper outlines the processes of knowledge enhancement and relationship extraction in greater detail.

We have significantly enhanced the data processing workflow and initial findings for our survey of the Galactic plane, known as Hi-GAL, and further developed pre-processing techniques. Initially, Hi-GAL, developed within the Herschel Survey, covered the inner regions of the Galactic plane, from longitudes -30° to +30°, and latitudes 20° to 40°, at frequencies of 665, 500, and 354 microns, using B, C, and L bands respectively. Our pre-processing workflow efficiently combines observations, incorporating corrections for instrument and beam effects, and addresses scan strategies using map-matching techniques to align data from overlapping fields. This enables reprocessing of archival data without relying on real-time processing methods. Hi-GAL, now available online, is a seamless full-sky survey, including its first data release. A new reduction pipeline has facilitated the production of over 100 million sources, and we have outlined the procedures for creating source, flux, and color catalogs. Hi-GAL, processed with the new pipeline, includes over 100 billion full-sky sources, and we provide examples of their properties.

The globular cluster NGC 2808 exhibits a notable range of helium-25 abundances within its variable stars, a characteristic that researchers believe is associated with multiple stellar populations with different metal contents. However, previous studies on the cluster's abundance of iron, based on limited data, have failed to reach a definitive conclusion. To address this, we employed high-resolution spectroscopy to measure the abundance of 10 elements in 12 blue giant members, members of either the blue horizontal branch or blue straggler populations. Our findings suggest a notable trend between the content of iron and helium-25 in stars, supporting the notion that the cluster's varying helium-25 abundances are linked to different metal contents of the population from which the stars originated.

One-dimensional confined environments, or single file systems, are often characterized by peculiar statistical patterns. When observing Brownian particles within these environments, researchers typically analyze two types of events: (1) a particle not exiting a certain domain over a certain time period, or (2) a particle leaving a certain domain and re-entering within a certain time frame. Previous studies examined the long term behavior of the dwell time, a measure of how long a particle stays outside a domain before re-entering. In contrast, our research focuses on the short term behavior of this time and identifies a distinct "initial exit time" period where the dwell time behavior deviates from its long term behavior. Additionally, our study investigates the initial exit duration statistics - a measure of the time it takes two particles to mutually re-enter one domain after leaving it. Through simulations and numerical analysis, our research reveals that single file statistics can be understood through the lens of entropy and that the initial exit duration statistics can be used to differentiate between entropic and non-entropic systems. Ultimately, our study provides a more comprehensive understanding of single file events and their statistical patterns.

Quantum mechanics poses a significant challenge in defining the process of measurement and the theoretical framework underpinning it. Various interpretations of quantum mechanics address this issue differently. This study focuses on the underlying principles and mathematical structure of quantum mechanics rather than its interpretation. It also assumes that information obtained from a quantum system's measurement follows the quantum version of Bayes' theorem, which resolves the contradiction between Bayesian inference and the Born rule. This approach leads to a set of equations representing a quantum information flow based on the algebraic properties of observables and states. These equations are formulated within a C*-algebra, a type of mathematical object where a positive linear functional serves as a key component of Bayesian inference. These equations are analogous to the von Neumann equation, a fundamental equation in quantum mechanics, and provide a framework for understanding quantum measurements in terms of information theory.

Recently, a novel approach to calculating the free energy of a quark-gluon plasma has gained attention due to its potential to utilize lattice QCD data more effectively. The method treats the free energy as a thermodynamic series in the density of quarks and gluons, expanding in powers of the chemical potential and baryon number, and captures non-perturbative effects through complex conditions. Each term in this series is weighted by a numerically determinable factor, and several terms have already been calculated using lattice QCD. By comparing the real and imaginary parts of the result to the series' predictions at higher orders, key features of the series can be identified. The approach is applicable at any level of strong coupling and for systems of both the same particle type (color neutral) and those involving the creation and annihilation of particle-antiparticle pairs. It may be used to study the quark-gluon plasma in a variety of environments such as the early stages of a heavy-ion collision, a photon-rich system created in a heavy-ion collision, or the core of a neutron star.

A moment's ago, I had the opportunity to participate in a discussion with the authors of the paper, where they explored the non-ignorability of certain components in the Steenrod algebra's cohomology groups for $k\geq 3$. This led me to a simple yet noteworthy observation which I feel warrants sharing.

A new experimental setup has been developed to capture images of space at a wavelength of 121.6 nm using a filter made of Lyman-alpha gas, which is much lighter than traditional liquid lithium. The conical shape of the gas film, which is about 100 micrometers to 300 micrometers in thickness at 10 cm away from a 10 cm diameter dipole depolarizer, allows for detailed calculations of its properties. By taking into account the gas pressure, depolarizer placement, and gas temperature, it is possible to precisely calculate the gas density, which depends heavily on temperature. At an optimal temperature of 300 K and a pressure of 100 Torr, the gas film has a reflectance of around 30% and a cut-off wavelength of approximately 105 nm. Additionally, this setup has a transmission bandwidth of about 12 nm and exhibits significant changes in reflectance when subjected to shifts as small as 0.1 nm.

This research investigates ideal distributed control strategies for linear time-invariant multi-agent systems exhibiting symmetrical interconnections. By representing these networks as graphs, we focus on the case where node symmetries align with edge symmetry, leading to the suggestion of graph filter controls as potential solutions. We demonstrate that symmetric graph filters can achieve optimal results under specific conditions which depend on the network structure and input signals. Notably, the proposed graph symmetry requirements are minimal and underlaying causes of network symmetries are clarified. To provide practical insights, we also examine the relationship between optimal graph filter controls and other existing control strategies in cases where optimal graph symmetry conditions are not met.

Retrieving and analyzing information from video is becoming increasingly vital due to the growing availability of video data online. To facilitate video analysis, the paper proposes a novel indexing system called Dynamic Picture Indexing (DPI). This system uses keyframes extracted from videos as search indices, allowing the full video to be searched by querying multiple of these index videos. A picture index is created by selecting a series of keyframes at non-un间隔 from the video, ensuring that videos of different lengths can be indexed uniformly. Notably, a search query may target a single video or multiple videos, and unlike traditional indexing methods, a picture index is dynamic and can be created on the fly from the video itself, rather than being created beforehand in a static index. To achieve efficient searching, the paper develops two retrieval algorithms to locate the video or videos that closely resemble the dynamic picture index in terms of overall visual similarity, content progression, and camera movement. Experimental results using a comprehensive video dataset demonstrate the system's effectiveness in efficiently locating the most similar videos or sets of videos to the given picture index.

This paper introduces a novel protocol, Echo-Verify, for secure communication over the Gaussian channel without requiring a shared secret key. Our research reveals that as the block length approaches infinity, there can be a non-zero rate at which messages are securely transmitted, with the error rate approaching zero as the signal-to-noise ratio increases towards a certain threshold determined by a special constant in mathematics. We develop another approach, the Causal-NonCausal channel model, which helps design efficient and secure coding schemes that exploit the differences in available information for the sender and receiver. The Causal-NonCausal channel has connections to a significant problem in information theory involving the transmission of information over a communication channel assisted by future information about the signal.

We demonstrate that 1D and 2C Josephson junction arrays in a one-dimensional landscape can support uniform quantum transport in the Aharonov-Bohm and Dicke limits, in the absence of a specific, well-defined quantum state. For certain washboard energies, where the relevant density of states remains constant, transport characteristics remain consistent regardless of the system's size. However, in other washboard energies, particularly near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, the relevant density of states varies significantly, resulting in size-dependent coupling between the parts of the system and large system-size dependence of conductivity. We also explain how near the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, DC conductivity exhibits system-size scaling consistent with thermal phase slips.

Building on DiNardo, Green, and Schneider (1989), researchers investigate shock effects on time series variables, specifically focusing on dynamic estimation in the short run and long run. The standard practice of truncating short-run estimates to calculate multi-step impulse response functions may not accurately reflect economic reality. DiNardo and friends' innovation of flexible local projections can be applied in this context to determine the optimal length of the short run, thereby minimizing estimation errors. The thesis examines this concept, investigates its theoretical underpinnings, and investigates the local projection's impact on inference. The research reveals that flexible projection can significantly alter standard error estimates, particularly when combined with heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent estimators. The findings hold particular significance for variables exhibiting persistent patterns. The effectiveness of flexible projection in improving short-run estimates may come at the cost of reduced long-run estimate accuracy. The accuracy of long-run estimates can be further compromised when the innovation to a persistent variable is present, specifically in the form of moving average processes of a certain order or higher. The research investigates how finite sample properties align with asymptotic predictions. The alignment varies by sector of the economy, but in most cases, there is a notable discrepancy between theoretical and practical outcomes. The alignment is influenced by the degree of time series persistence and the length of the short-run period. The research specifically highlights the need for a thorough examination of the trade-offs involved in flexible projection when estimating short-run periods, particularly

The behavior of the electromagnetic field's quantum vacuum in the presence of a charge moving through a magnetic field is examined. By simulating the charge's motion using operator techniques in the framework of quantum field theory, this study reveals a counterintuitive result: a charge moving through a magnetic field experiences a self-generated radiation reaction force opposing its motion, due to the angular momentum vacuum inducing a torque that influences the charge's dynamics in the system.

The traditional task of Named Entity Recognition (NER) involves only detecting entity categories and assigning start and stop indices. A more advanced task, Fine-grained NER, breaks down broader categories into more specific ones. However, current methods struggle with accurately identifying nested entities and pre-trained language models often fail to capture fine-grained entity categories. To overcome these limitations, we propose FGNET-RH, a novel framework for refining NER in a 2D manifold. It consists of a primary model that performs initial NER and a secondary framework for refining it. A log-normalizing cross-entropy loss is introduced to adapt the initial model for refinement within the 2D manifold. Unlike traditional methods, FGNET-RH allows for flexible refinement of any category and its subcategories, while also eliminating the need for a teacher-student model, making it computationally efficient. To evaluate its performance, we introduce the REFINER, a benchmark dataset for dynamic refinement NER. Results show that FGNET-RH significantly outperforms existing methods, with an F1-score improvement of 1.02% and 2.01% for general and nested entity classification tasks, respectively, on fine-grained categories, and it can adapt to the dynamic refinement of any category and its subcategories.

Let's define the class $\mathcal{U}$ as comprising functions belonging to the family $\mathcal{S}$ that meet the criterion $|a_2| \leq a_2^* < 2$. We establish specific Hankel determinant constraints for the class $\mathcal{U}$ and a broader category $\mathcal{S}$ with sufficient precision for practical application.

Emerging technologies like virtualization and cloud computing have significantly impacted data centers, enabling cost-effective and efficient resource allocation strategies for businesses. However, growing demands on these resources have led to increased energy consumption, necessitating the development of new strategies to manage this load. In this study, a novel approach called Prepartition is introduced, which involves dividing a cluster into smaller subclusters and distributing workloads evenly across them to optimize energy usage. We evaluate the Prepartition strategy using our HPV framework, comparing it against two baseline load distribution methods - random and balanced scheduling - and demonstrating improved results in terms of completing more jobs and reducing energy consumption when not utilizing the prepartition strategy, and achieving substantial improvements over balanced scheduling when utilizing it.

In many strategic environments, predicting player behavior by inferring equilibrium concepts can be more valuable than other forms of prediction. Recent research has demonstrated success in this area using data-driven methods. However, many current strategies involve a two-step process: first learning the target environment's properties, and then using that information to derive the desired predictions. This indirect approach, however, poses challenges when it comes to generalizing to new situations.

This paper proposes a novel method for directly inferring fixed-point or Nash-paintings from observations within the target environment, thereby making predictions in unseen situations. This technique relies on a neural network, called a Fixed Point Network (FPN), which learns the operations of a well-known algorithm, such as Policy Iteration or Best Response Dynamics. By adjusting the parameters of the FNN to match the target environment, the FPN can converge to the correct fixed-point or Nash-paintings, thereby yielding the correct predictions.

Our results demonstrate that FPNs trained using a reinforcement learning approach can learn both fixed-point and Nash-paintings, and can generalize well to new situations. This capability is particularly valuable when the target environment is complex, such as in games or other strategic environments. Additionally, our method allows for the direct comparison of FPNs with other prediction techniques, and our experiments show that FPNs can outperform several baselines, particularly in complex settings.

This research investigates the notion of causal influence, particularly in terms of the maximum impact a variable can have on another, beyond their shared background factors. Unlike statistical dependence, which can be inferred from observational data, the concept of infinite-level causal influence requires interventions. A notable limitation of past studies on this topic is that they rely solely on non-directional measures, thereby obscuring the direction of the influence. To address this gap, we introduce new, directed, and non-parametric measures of infinite-level causal influence, accompanied by the development of techniques to intervene on unobserved variables and estimate these measures in practical scenarios. Our simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of these new measures in distinguishing between variables that are merely correlated and those that are directly connected in a causal framework. Moreover, these measures outperform existing non-parametric methods in applications to real-world data, such as predicting outcomes in baseball games.

This study proposes a technique for anticipating stealth attacks on a closed-loop system with limited predictability. When an unsuspected attack commences, initial system measurements become distorted, and the prediction accuracy declines. To counteract this, the paper suggests modifying the prediction horizon and gains once stealth attack detection triggers. Optimized new parameters can minimize the effect of initial detection error, thus enhancing prediction precision. It's also demonstrated that adjusting the prediction parameters can conceivably keep the system stable up to a point of maximum latency. Numerical examples are used to illustrate the proposed predictive control strategy.

This paper introduces GAE-ISumm, a new pre-trained Graph Neural Network model for generating abstractive summaries of documents written in the 8 major Indian languages. Currently available models for abstractive summarization are primarily designed for European languages and fall short in handling the complexity of Indian languages. To bridge this gap, we develop GAE-ISumm by fine-tuning the Graph Attention Network model and adapting it for Indian languages by using machine-translated datasets. Experimental results across multiple datasets show that GAE-ISumm outperforms other state-of-the-art models for Indian languages and achieves results comparable to pre-trained models like GAT and BART for European languages. We make the model and related code publicly available for further research and application.
We explore the characteristics of S-rings of Noether type within group theory.

A recent study suggested that the five stars exhibiting acceleration, S2, DSS J08525-1161,
HD 147886, DSS J1543-1423, and DSS J1543-1429, may have hidden massive companions.
This claim was contested by other researchers, who proposed the masses of these companions
could be significantly lower, within the 1-10 $M_{\odot}$ range. In order to test this hypothesis,
we employed the N-body simulation tool REBOUND, simulating the interactions between these
star systems and their potential companions. In simulations, we modeled the S2 system, 
featuring two massive black holes and four stars, as well as the three potential stellar
companion systems of S2, S2hd, and DSS J08525-1161. This study demonstrates that the 
configurations of the S2 system and S2hd allowing for significant acceleration are restricted, 
with masses of companions less than 5 $M_{\odot}$ and distances less than 1 $r_{\rm H}$, 
where $r_{\rm H}$ is the radius of the Hill sphere.

A widely accepted approach for unsupervised dimensionality reduction is the use of Autoencoders (AEs), which compress high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional representation and then reconstruct the original data. The traditional SAE, however, lacks the direct application of a statistical model, a shortcoming addressed in our Variational Bayesian Autoencoders (VAEs) which incorporate a stochastic encoder and latent covariance matrix, explicitly modeling the likelihood of the observed data through the reconstruction of the input data. Furthermore, we incorporate a Gaussian prior and a Gaussian inverse-Wishart posterior for the covariance matrix, enabling the use of variational inference to derive the variational posterior. The proposed VAE, dubbed the Minimal Square Variational Bayesian Autoencoders (MSVAE), differs from the standard VAE by incorporating an additional regularization term related to the variance of the encoder, a term that enhances the model's performance when dealing with highly correlated data, as seen in brain imaging data. Our model, tested on the MNIST dataset, surpasses existing models by CRCAE and RVBAE, particularly in highly correlated datasets.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things has led to widespread deployment of smart home devices. However, this also poses a significant challenge in effectively monitoring smart home gadgets. Filling this monitoring gap is crucial for ensuring users' safety and well-being. In response, this study proposes a blockchain-based smart home monitoring solution that uses a private blockchain network and a consensus algorithm tailored to meet smart home monitoring needs. A blockchain-based database and smart contracts are created to track indoor air quality sensors, allowing for real-time monitoring. Furthermore, the system incorporates machine learning-based image classification and a mobile app to localize and display data on a real-time map. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed blockchain-based monitoring solution is a practical and reliable approach to keeping smart home device owners informed.

This research introduces a novel method for reducing the bit-depth of large MIBs in 5G NR systems. The approach involves a two-stage process. The first stage involves a neural network that extracts critical information from the L-value, which is then quantized to a smaller bit-depth. The second stage quantizes the output of the first stage to further reduce the bit-depth. The output is then encoded using a modified version of the Gray code, which minimizes the effects of the quantization process when signals are weak. The approach's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulation results, which show significant improvements in the large MIB detection performance when combined with quantization and Gray-coded modulation.

Upward planarity drawings of partial directed graphs are characterized by the fact that all edges have zero y-component when the source has, and we investigate the complexity of creating such drawings when parameterized by the count of sources with infinite y-component. For the issue of bounded-separated graphs, the most significant result is the establishment of a fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithm based on the number of strongly connected components. This bounded-separated graph class is defined as containing only tree-like components, and it has been proven that its components have limited size when parameterized by the maximum degree of any vertex. This is achieved through the development of an algorithm with O(n^2k^2) edges, where n is the number of vertices, and k is the maximum degree of any vertex. This result is achieved by constructing a bounded-separated graph with O(nk^2) edges, and it has been shown that such a graph can be drawn in an FPT manner when parameterized by the number of vertices of infinite y-coordinate, under specific constraints. This research presents multiple algorithms, the most time-efficient being O(nq^3log^3q), and it establishes the condition for such an algorithm to exist as fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by the number of vertices of infinite y-coordinate. This research provides evidence for the difficulty of the issue, as it presents an example of a graph that resists being drawn in an upward planar manner when the number of vertices exceeds a cubic function of the

Crowdsourced data is often marred by significant noise, hindering the development of reliable machine learning models. This issue can be addressed by leveraging various ensemble methods combined with uncertainty metrics to pinpoint and discard unreliable responses from crowdsourced datasets. This research introduces a novel, systematic approach for analyzing and extracting knowledge from noisy, crowdsourced data sources. The proposed approach involves two main stages: Firstly, it employs an ensemble method that integrates multiple machine learning models, and secondly, it utilizes a data filtering mechanism based on uncertainty metrics to eliminate low-quality responses. The present research showcases the effectiveness of a novel ensemble method known as the Human Softmax Ensemble (HSE), and demonstrates its ability to enhance system reliability in a real-world, low-resource environment. Specifically, the research reveals that the HSE method, when combined with two entropic uncertainty metrics, enables the systematic analysis of noisy crowdsourced datasets. The Human Softmax Ensemble (HSE) method is an innovative ensemble technique, and its human-centric design aims to replicate human decision-making strategies. This method integrates individual predictions from multiple machine learning models, and aggregates their outputs through a soft-max function, yielding calibrated, probabilistic outputs. The Human Softmax Ensemble (HSE) method, along with the incorporation of uncertainty metrics, empowers researchers to effectively identify and remove noisy responses from crowdsourced datasets.

For semiflows with rapid mixing properties applied to compact manifolds, the exponential rate at which the transfer operators' norms in $L^p$ spaces diminish can be significantly improved. This improvement is particularly evident in cases where the mixing rate surpasses a certain threshold, in which scenario we can accurately determine the diminishing rate of the transfer operators' norms.

This paper proposes a novel framework for minor strength-2 covering arrays, specifically CA-NM(2; g1, t1, g2, t2, n, s), which is shown to be equivalent to paired binary arrays. We provide both upper and lower bounds for this new structure. A specific case of CA-NM(2; 2, g1, 3, 2, n, s) is proposed with this paper, along with constructive methods to generate this new type of testing suite.

Nonlocal versions of traditional game theory problems, with their high entanglement and strategic flexibility, have been investigated. It has been found that when these nonlocal games involve certain properties, like being fully interconnected and affected by noise, their winning strategies can actually be determined accurately and efficiently through a detailed mathematical approach.

A recent paper presented a novel approach to automated crash replication through guided genetic algorithms, showcasing its effectiveness on real-world driving scenarios with significant differences in speed, time of day, and lighting conditions, resulting in a success rate of over 90%. However, given that most crash replication research has relied on a limited set of test cases, it is challenging to assess the generalizability of these methods. Utilizing actual crash data from non-overlapping insurance companies from two geographically distant states, this study evaluates the potential limitations of the existing guided algorithm and crash replication research more broadly, highlighting the need for diverse testing environments. Moreover, alternative solutions to increase the robustness of crash replication methods are suggested, such as leveraging larger, publicly available datasets or research-based synthetic crash data, to assess the potential limitations of the existing research approach.

Theoretical predictions suggest a complex pattern of vortex dynamics occurs near the melting point of vortices in ultra-thin, doped $YbCoxCe1-xCu2$ crystals. Experimental data collected from these ultra-thin crystals using scanning SQUID microscopy at temperatures just below the critical temperature ($T_c$) and under high magnetic fields ($9.4$ Tesla) showed a previously unobserved phenomenon: the formation of a two-dimensional grid consisting of two vortices. This grid consists of parallel rows of vortices running along the crystal's c-axis, separated by single-vortex channels. Furthermore, the properties of this two-vortex structure differ significantly from single-vortex configurations in the same material, displaying a high degree of internal flexibility and static behavior. These findings support the idea that there is a distinct phase transition occurring near $H=0$ Tesla, involving a shift in the arrangement of vortices within the cuprate superconductor, as predicted by theory.

For the first time, researchers have theoretically analyzed thermal photon directional anisotropy in the quark-gluon plasma with variable viscosity under high-energy collisions, employing an isotropic thermal bath model to simulate quark and gluon distribution up to a temperature of 350 MeV. The study considers both single and double scattering contributions derived from finite temperature perturbation theory and discovers that significant directional anisotropy effects emerge at lower temperatures and transverse momentum values. The results suggest that modeling assumptions about quark and gluon distributions can have significant implications for transport coefficients, calling for the creation of quantum kinetic theories with variable viscosity in simulations. The study also concludes that the medium's directional anisotropy serves as a clear indicator for the properties of the quark-gluon plasma produced in collisions.

For kagome lattices, a comprehensive classification of all possible unconstrained magnetic settings has been achieved, which includes 162 distinct arrangements, with 99 of these being uniquely immutable. The number of magnetic configurations in triangular lattices is significantly fewer at just 59, of which only 26 are consistently invariant. A detailed examination of possible interactions up to the 4-th nearest neighbors, specifically for ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic coupling, has been carried out using group theory for kagome and triangular lattices. The results show that there are a total of 113 distinct magnetic arrangements for kagome lattices, while in triangular lattices, a total of 23 magnetic configurations exist.

In large-scale intervention effect identification studies, such as those involving A/B testing, controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) under dependence is crucial. However, the effective management of FBD has been limited by the lack of accurate knowledge of dependence between intervention effects. We propose a new method to control the FBD in these studies, even when dependence is unknown, by assuming only non-negative correlation among positive intervention effects. This approach is based on an improved model that takes into account variable selection bias. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, the method's validity is confirmed, and the associated challenges, such as inflated variance and computational complexity caused by sub-sampling, are addressed. Finally, the method is applied to a real-world dataset, specifically the interventional effects on the click-through rate for different words in Google's search results.

This paper utilizes differential geometry to create a mathematical model of celestial bodies expanding according to Hubble's law. A novel approach to expansion in a non-Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metric is explored, outlining a procedure to construct the associated expansion fields. Conditions for the existence of these fields, along with their classifications and relationships to symmetries, are identified. Furthermore, this article offers insights into the expansion dynamics of specific astronomical objects, including stars, galaxies, and clusters.

The anomaly in the $c\mu$ measurement is successfully explained by the type-X 2HDM's heavy Higgs mediations for both the $a_\mu$ and $R_D^\ell$ anomalies, eliminating the need for $\mathcal{O}(1)$ third-generation Yukawa coupling. The $\Delta \alpha$ and $\Delta M_{Z^0}$ contributions from the type-X 2HDM's light scalar mediations are significantly small, making the Higgs trilinear coupling negligible and the Higgs sector consistent with the electroweak precision tests. The Fitsum-2022 $c\mu$ measurement is slightly lower than the previous measurement but still within the anomalous range and can be accommodated by the 2HDM light scalar mediations, reducing the need for heavy Higgs contributions, although a 100-1000 GeV Higgs mass region remains viable, near the boundaries of $\Delta \alpha$ and $\Delta M_{Z^0}$ contributions.

Our SWIFTER system is designed to uncover hidden concepts in texts by identifying related phrases that signify the same idea. This package enhances existing automated concept discovery methods by leveraging automatic query reformulation, driven by crowd-sourced knowledge, to locate underlying ideas. It begins by creating a reformulated query based on a document's title and then uses these to locate new concepts. The system's integration with crowdsourced data sources allows SWIFTER to cross-reference its findings with SWIS, a comprehensive swarm intelligence system, ensuring consistency. The package includes two types of query reformulation strategies - one based on crowd-sourced sources like Wikipedia and the other using the document's own vocabulary via n-gram analysis. The effectiveness of SWIFTER is evaluated through a benchmark study comparing its findings to those of SWIS, revealing superior performance in terms of both human and machine evaluators.

This article presents a novel method for measuring synchronization within conversational speech interactions, focusing on the pragmatic aspect of communication. Unlike existing methods, we adopt an unsupervised approach, allowing for distance learning directly from speech data without relying on explicit annotations. By addressing limitations in current pragmatic alignment metrics that fail to capture conversational nuances, we introduce a novel metric that correlates speaker proximity with linguistic similarity. To facilitate speech recognition and processing, we develop a deep neural network to learn speaker identity from speech signals. The results obtained using the proposed method on conversational speech data are comparable to those of state-of-the-art metrics, indicating its potential effectiveness. Moreover, we observe a notable correlation between speaker and linguistic proximity.

A version 2 of the Radio Continuum and Spectral Energy Distribution depiction tool, RCSEDv2, is presented, incorporating essential features for analyzing imaging and spectral energy distribution data. The tool, designed as a versatile all-in-one platform, spans from millimeter to optical wavelengths and includes capabilities for continuum analysis, spectral energy distribution plotting, and fitting both continuous and discrete spectra. To accommodate various data sources, RCSEDv2 has been optimized for data from the VLA and SEDs from the SED-MP database. The tool has been successfully used in examining the spectral energy distributions of galaxies, particularly in the context of the COSMOS2015 and COSMOS-3.6G surveys, demonstrating its potential for efficient data evaluation. The release of RCSEDv2 alongside its comprehensive user guide aims to significantly impact the efficiency of spectral energy distribution analysis.

Human action recognition through temporal understanding is a fundamental aspect of human-computer interaction. A major challenge in recursive human action recognition is getting sufficient, accurately labeled data. This problem hampers the development of efficient, effective algorithms for unattended video recognition. This research proposes a novel, unsupervised recursive algorithm called SSCAP, designed to tackle this issue by leveraging self-supervision and consistency regularization. Drawing inspiration from human learning, SSCAP formulates a self-supervised task centered on co-occurrence relationships between actions, effectively circumventing the need for extensive labeled data. Furthermore, SSCAP offers an innovative approach to recursive algorithms through the development of two novel recurrence constraint rules, enabling more accurate human action recognition. Experiments conducted on five challenging datasets demonstrate that SSCAP performs competitively against state-of-the-art models while significantly reducing the need for extensive labeled data.

A team of researchers has used the present algebra to study the properties of a specific type of pentaquark called the $C\bar{c}u d$ state with a mass of around 4.4 GeV, which was recently created in a collision involving beauty particles by the LHCb experiment. The team has identified the spin and parity of a pair of these quark states and found that there are additional quark configurations within the same system. The researchers have also examined the decay patterns of a related state, which was not observed in an experiment, and found that it decays primarily into a J/ψ and a Kaon particle. The study has opened the door to further research into a second type of park quark state, which could be found in a decay mode involving a proton and an anti-Kon particle, with a high probability of occurrence.

The paper addresses the concerns surrounding students' assessment in software testing education, where traditional code review methods may not effectively gauge students' understanding of concepts. An alternative method called Inquir-Based Conceptual Responses (IBCR) is introduced, facilitating teachers to evaluate students' knowledge of testing concepts and their ability to identify defects. A classroom-based study compared IBCR assessments to traditional code review methods and assessed their reliability in predicting identification of defects in familiar software. A reliable IBCR assessment, employing a closed-world testing scenario, demonstrated a significant correlation between these assessment types and identified defect localization in code. An open-world scenario, however, yielded inconsistent results. A theoretical framework explaining these findings was proposed, highlighting the importance of instructor and student experience on assessment outcomes.

Domain adaptation seeks to address challenges arising from distribution shifts between a source domain with domain-specific labels and structures and a target domain lacking labels due to these shifts. Traditional approaches for tackling domain adaptation rely heavily on labeled data and domain domain-specific methods, which become ineffective when faced with unlabeled target domains and new domains with novel distribution shifts. Theory transfer, a novel framework, aims to tackle these challenges by leveraging a theoretically sound, domain-invariant representation space to accurately classify the target domain without relying on domain-specific domain knowledge. A new semi-supervised theory transfer framework, which involves the source and target domains, is proposed to further improve this approach. This method relies on a generative model to generate a theoretical, domain-invariant representation and utilizes the source and target distributions. A new, generative model is introduced to generate this theory, which enables the accurate classification of the target domain. To address the challenges arising from these shifts, a generative model is proposed to transfer the source distribution into the theory. This method involves two generative models: one for translating the source distribution into the theory and another for reconstructing the original distribution from the theory. By minimizing the distance between these models and the original distribution, a robust and domain-invariant theory is obtained.
